content: Sanitary sewer overflow (SSO) refers to the release of untreated sewage into the environment, bypassing wastewater treatment systems. This phenomenon, also called Wet Weather Overflow, is particularly relevant in developed nations with extensive sewage treatment infrastructure. SSOs are caused by several factors, including the infiltration of excessive stormwater into sewer systems during heavy rainfall, ruptures or blockages in sewer lines, malfunctions in pumping stations due to mechanical or electrical failures, and human errors at treatment facilities. In countries with near-total domestic wastewater treatment, such as the United States, Japan, the United Kingdom, and parts of Europe, SSOs are considered significant failures in environmental water resource management. Historically, the dangers of improperly discharged raw sewage have been recognized for centuries. In 16th-century England, King Henry VIII mandated that sewage troughs in London remain flowing to prevent stagnation before reaching the River Thames. However, the concept of SSOs only emerged in the 19th century with the advent of wastewater treatment systems in parts of Europe and America. Public concern over SSOs grew in the 20th century, particularly during the environmental movement of the 1960s. Following the Clean Water Act, the 1980s saw billions of dollars invested in upgrading sewer systems. By the 1990s, countries like Japan, the UK, and others in Europe began addressing their own SSO issues. The scale of the problem is significant. The U.S. government aims to upgrade municipal treatment and collection systems to limit overflow events to no more than once every five years in any given community. Achieving this goal is estimated to cost $88 billion, in addition to the $10 billion already spent. Although untreated sewage from SSOs accounts for less than 0.1% of all treated sewage in the U.S., the total volume still amounts to billions of gallons annually, leading to thousands of cases of gastrointestinal illness. Advanced nations in Europe and Japan report similar or slightly higher rates of SSOs. From an engineering perspective, the most common cause of SSOs is heavy rainfall, which leads to stormwater infiltration into sewer systems. This issue is particularly prevalent in older cities with aging infrastructure, such as Paris, London, Stockholm, New York, and Oakland. Other causes include power outages that disable lift station pumps, mechanical failures in treatment plants, and human errors. Decentralized failures, such as blockages in collection sewer lines caused by debris, ruptures, or tree root intrusion, can also lead to overflows. Identifying the exact location of such failures is challenging in urban areas with extensive sewer networks unless costly monitoring systems are in place. The health and ecological consequences of SSOs are substantial. Human health impacts include thousands of cases of gastrointestinal illness annually, though fatalities from single overflow events are rare. Ecologically, SSOs can cause fish kills, harm to plankton and other aquatic microorganisms, and increased turbidity and decreased dissolved oxygen in water bodies. These effects can cascade through ecosystems, potentially impacting higher life forms such as marine mammals, including seals and sea lions, which are known to suffer from pathogenic outbreaks linked to SSOs. Globally, the issue of SSOs is dwarfed by the scale of untreated sewage discharge in underdeveloped nations. While developed countries like the U.S., Canada, Western Europe, Australia, and Japan grapple with SSO prevention, underdeveloped nations discharge approximately 20,000 times more raw sewage into the environment. For instance, China, despite being highly industrialized, discharges 55% of its sewage untreated. In Tehran, Iran, most of the population's sewage is injected untreated into groundwater. In Venezuela, 97% of sewage is released raw into the environment. Sub-Saharan Africa, lacking wastewater treatment infrastructure, faces severe public health crises, including high infant mortality rates. Collectively, underdeveloped nations discharge an estimated 100 trillion gallons (380 km³) of untreated sewage annually, highlighting a stark disparity in public health and environmental management between developed and underdeveloped regions.
